cim: The world is waging a “Third World War” through Artificial Intelligence - what role can Egypt play?
cim_eredeti: The world is waging a “Third World War” through Artificial Intelligence - what role can Egypt play?
szoveg_eredeti:
Technology and the struggle for global influence have become increasingly intertwined at a time when Artificial Intelligence (AI) has grown from a mere economic tool into a defining component of national power and countries’ capacity for strategic deterrence.

This has made the development of AI capabilities and the regulation of their use matters of national security, particularly amid the growing military applications of these technologies and documented evidence of their use in the genocidal war waged in the Gaza Strip.

Against this backdrop, New Giza University, in collaboration with the University of Glasgow, hosted a conference titled “The New Wealth of Nations: AI Is Fundamentally Reshaping the Global Economy.”

The event, bringing together a distinguished group of diplomats and academics, examined the implications of the technological revolution for the global balance of power, the future of the economy, and the development of ethical and institutional frameworks to govern the use of intelligent technologies.

Egypt emerged prominently in the conference discussions as a country well positioned to play an influential role in the emerging international order.

This potential stems from its geographic location, strategic weight, and role in managing Middle Eastern crises, as well as opportunities to expand its presence in global trade, investment, and production chains, and contribute to shaping the rules governing cybersecurity and artificial intelligence.

Amid competition among the United States, China, and the European Union, alongside the rise of blocs such as BRICS, participants raised questions about Egypt’s ability to help move countries across the region from a position of vulnerability to international conflicts and transformations to that of active partners in shaping their future.

They stressed that stability in the Middle East remains contingent on a just settlement of the Palestinian issue, while shifts in the global economy are creating new opportunities for Egypt, provided it develops the technological and institutional capabilities needed to compete.

The forum marked the 10th anniversary of New Giza University and the 250th anniversary of the publication of The Wealth of Nations by Scottish economist Adam Smith, widely regarded as the “father of modern economics.”

His ideas on the division of labor and free trade laid important foundations for understanding the growth of production, wealth, and societal prosperity.

The opening session featured discussions among leaders, officials, and academics who drew on Smith’s intellectual legacy to interpret contemporary transformations.

They warned of technology becoming an instrument of conflict among major powers and highlighted the risks of wealth and influence becoming concentrated in the hands of a limited number of companies and countries.

They also underscored the need to redefine the role of the state in regulating markets, protecting people, and ensuring a fairer distribution of the benefits of technological progress.

Egypt’s former ambassador to the European Union in Brussels, Raouf Adly, said that AI had become a new arena of competition among major powers, as international rivalry shifts from traditional military capabilities towards technological ownership, knowledge production, and data processing.

He described the ongoing cyber confrontation as a “Third World War” being waged through different means, warning that the region risks being left out of this equation.

He further cautioned against the use of these intelligent technologies without ethical safeguards to protect humanity.

Adly ruled out the possibility that international relations would remain confined to a bipolar framework dominated by major powers.

Instead, he predicted a growing role for regional blocs and cross-regional alliances, potentially creating opportunities to reinvigorate European partnerships with the Middle East amid tensions between Washington and Brussels.

He stated that Egypt was well positioned to occupy a pivotal place in these emerging dynamics.

Adly based his assessment on the historical turning points that followed the two world wars, noting that the First World War led to the establishment of the League of Nations, while the Second World War gave rise to the United Nations.

Major wars, explained, have historically transformed the structure and institutions of the international system, raising the possibility of another reshaping of international relations in the near future.

Adly also discussed his experience in negotiations over the Egypt-European Partnership Agreement, which was linked to the Madrid Peace Conference and aimed at building economic and trade relations that would pave the way for a broad free-trade area.

However, the stalled peace process prevented this vision from fully achieving its objectives, leaving the agreements closer to a model of “managed free trade” than to the complete liberalization of commercial exchange.

He argued that tensions between the US and Europe could prompt European capitals to redirect part of their economic and strategic relationships towards regions beyond the continent, particularly the Middle East, Africa, Asia, and Latin America. This, he said, would give Egypt an opportunity to strengthen its partnerships, given its geopolitical position and its role in managing regional crises.

Adly added that developments in the Middle East since October 7, 2023, had once again highlighted the importance of Egypt’s role in containing crises.

Cairo’s influence, he said, rests on a measured and precise diplomatic approach, as well as international recognition of its position in regional stability calculations.

He stressed that any vision for the region’s future would remain incomplete without a just settlement of the Palestinian issue.

On economic transformations, Adly cautioned against reducing BRICS to an alliance seeking to overthrow the dollar or confront the United States. Instead, he viewed the bloc as reflecting a broader shift towards international multipolarity and creating opportunities to redirect trade and cooperation across regions.

He cited the dollar’s continued dominance in approximately 80 percent of global transactions and China’s foreign exchange reserves, estimated at around $3.2 trillion, arguing that these figures do not support simplistic assumptions that Beijing intends to abandon the US currency.

Concluding his remarks, Adly linked current transformations to the legacy of economist Adam Smith, arguing that the rise of protectionist policies had harmed international trade and that the global economy was moving towards a more regulated model, which he described as “managed free trade.”

This, he said, reflects a shift away from the concept of the market’s “invisible hand” towards a greater role for the “visible hand” of government policies and organized intervention.

Former Egyptian Prime Minister Ahmed Nazif linked the transformations that AI is bringing to the global economy with the future of development in Egypt.

He stressed that the diversity of the Egyptian economy and the country’s location at the crossroads of three continents offer opportunities to attract investment and strengthen its presence in international production and trade chains.

He explained that artificial intelligence is not merely an advancement in production tools, but a transformation that is redefining wealth, economic value, and competitiveness.

This, he said, makes it necessary to establish ethical rules governing its applications and protecting people from potential harm.

Nazif called for subjecting AI applications to what he described as “meta-rules”: fundamental ethical principles that should precede the rules governing machines and prevent them from killing, lying, or cheating.

He stressed that any program violating these principles should be stopped.
